title: Best–worst scaling

definition.text: Best–worst scaling is a survey choice method in which respondents pick the best and the worst item from a subset of a longer list.

facts.text: Jordan Louviere invented it in 1987 at the University of Alberta, as a form of choice modelling or discrete choice experiment.
The task is repeated with subsets varied by a statistical design, and choices are usually analysed with a random utility model.
Because respondents choose rather than rate, it avoids scale-use bias and stops every item being rated 'quite important'.
It is hard to know how to combine best and worst answers when people use different decision rules for each.

title: Cheap talk

definition.text: In game theory, cheap talk is costless communication between players whose messages do not directly change the game's payoffs.

facts.text: Cheap talk is non-binding and cannot be verified by a third party, so a speaker could lie freely but may choose not to.
It differs from signalling, where sending some messages can be costly for the sender.
In a coordination game a round of cheap talk can help players reach better outcomes, but in the Prisoner's Dilemma it is ignored.

notes: The page covers only the game-theory sense; nothing in the dossier links it to cheap-talk scripts used against hypothetical bias in stated-preference surveys, the likely reason it was seeded here.

definition.text: The Exxon Valdez oil spill was a major environmental disaster in Prince William Sound, Alaska, on March 24, 1989.

facts.text: The supertanker Exxon Valdez struck Bligh Reef and spilled more than 10 million US gallons of crude oil over the next few days.
It was the first case where contingent valuation surveys were used in a quantitative assessment of damages, and use of the technique spread from there.
Existence values were part of the legal damage assessment after the spill.
An Anchorage jury awarded $287 million in actual damages and $5 billion in punitive damages, which an appeals court ordered reduced.

title: Latent class model

definition.text: A latent class model is a statistical model that sorts multivariate discrete data into hidden groups, or classes.

facts.text: It assumes the data come from a mixture of distributions, with the variables independent within each class.
It is called latent because each data point's class is not observed.
For example, answers to a political questionnaire could reveal latent classes corresponding to political groups.

notes: The page never mentions choice modelling or valuation; its use to find preference groups in choice experiments is not covered by the dossier.

definition.text: Meta-regression is a meta-analysis that uses regression to combine and compare findings from many studies while adjusting for study characteristics.

facts.text: It aims to reconcile conflicting studies or confirm consistent ones.
Fixed-effect versions assume the studies do not really differ, while mixed-effect versions allow for variation between studies and are often the most flexible choice.
It has been applied to the value of a statistical life, energy and water policy, and price elasticities for water and energy.
It is increasingly used to weigh evidence across many cost-benefit studies of a policy or programme.

definition.text: Mixed logit is a fully general statistical model for analysing discrete choices, in which tastes are allowed to vary randomly between people.

facts.text: It overcomes three limits of standard logit: it allows random taste variation, unrestricted substitution patterns, and correlation in unobserved factors over time.
Unlike standard logit, it does not impose the restrictive independence of irrelevant alternatives property.
With suitable specification it can approximate any random utility model of discrete choice to any accuracy.
Its choice probability has no closed form, so it must be estimated by simulation, drawing repeatedly from the taste distribution.

definition.text: Multinomial logistic regression is a statistical method that predicts the probabilities of more than two unordered outcomes from a set of explanatory variables.

facts.text: It is also called the multinomial logit, softmax regression or the maximum entropy classifier, among other names.
In discrete choice theory, each outcome's score is read as the utility a person gets from choosing it, with a random part standing for unmodelled factors.
Used for choices, it assumes independence of irrelevant alternatives: the odds between two options do not depend on what other options are present.
Many psychology studies show that people often violate this assumption.
In best–worst scaling studies it is often the first stage of analysis, giving average utilities for items.

definition.text: A probit model is a regression model for a dependent variable that can take only two values, built on the normal distribution.

facts.text: It estimates the probability that an observation with given characteristics falls into one of the two categories, the same problem logistic regression handles.
It can be motivated as a latent variable model, with the outcome showing whether an unobserved variable is positive.
It is usually estimated by maximum likelihood.
Chester Bliss coined the term in 1934, though the basic model goes back to Fechner in 1860.

definition.text: A random utility model describes a person's preferences when their choices are not fixed but depend on a random, unobserved state.

facts.text: Classic economics assumes a rational person picks the alternative with the highest utility, which can be inferred from observed choices.
In practice people facing the same alternatives may choose differently, so their choices look random to an observer.
The model gives each person a distribution over utility functions rather than a single one, and assumes rational behaviour given the hidden state.
Choice experiments assume how often item A is chosen over item B measures how much it is preferred.
A popular version was developed by Luce and Plackett.

definition.text: Scope neglect is a cognitive bias in which the value people place on a problem does not grow in proportion to its size.

facts.text: In one study people were willing to pay $80, $78 and $88 to save 2,000, 20,000 or 200,000 migrating birds from drowning in oil ponds.
Other willingness-to-pay studies have found a logarithmic relationship or no relationship to the size of the harm.
Daniel Kahneman explains it as judgment by prototype: people price a mental image, such as one oil-soaked bird, rather than the number affected.
It is a specific form of extension neglect, closely linked to the 'mass numbing' studied by Paul Slovic.

title: Hypothetical bias

definition.text: Hypothetical bias is the distortion in values people state in surveys about goods they do not actually have to pay for or give up.

facts.text: A public health study found hypothetical bias is greater when people have less information about a good and information is costly.
Stated willingness to pay is lower when hypothetical bias is high, widening the gap between willingness to accept and willingness to pay.
John A. List studied whether explicit warnings remove hypothetical bias in elicitation procedures.

definition.text: The bell-shaped probability distribution defined by a mean, which sets its location, and a variance, which sets its squared scale.

facts.text: The standard normal distribution is the case with mean 0 and variance 1; any normal variable can be built by scaling it by the standard deviation and shifting it by the mean.
About 68% of values lie within one standard deviation of the mean, about 95% within two and about 99.7% within three: the 68-95-99.7 or 3-sigma rule.
The distribution is symmetric around its mean, which is also its mode and median.
Its density is written with the Greek letter phi and its cumulative distribution function with capital Phi; the quantile function of the standard normal is the probit function.
Among all distributions with a given mean and variance, it has the maximum entropy, and it is the only one whose cumulants beyond the mean and variance are zero.
Any linear combination of independent normal variables is itself normal, and the sum of squares of independent standard normals has a chi-squared distribution.

Occurrences are loosely exact, approximate (explained by the central limit theorem) or merely assumed; Ioannidis warns that using normal standard deviations to validate findings leaves non-normal phenomena untested.

title: Central limit theorem
article: Normal distribution#Related distributions > Central limit theorem

definition.text: Under fairly common conditions, the sum of many random variables is approximately normally distributed.

facts.text: It applies to independent, identically distributed variables with the same arbitrary distribution, finite variance and zero mean; the scaled mean approaches a normal distribution as the number of variables grows.
It explains why approximately normal distributions turn up in so many situations.
